definition: A measure mu on a measurable space (X, F) is a function mu: F -> [0, infinity] that is countably additive: mu(union of disjoint A_i) = sum mu(A_i), and mu(empty set) = 0. A measure assigns 'size' to sets in a sigma-algebra. The triple (X, F, mu) is called a measure space. A measure is finite if mu(X) < infinity; sigma-finite if X is a countable union of sets with finite measure.

contrasts.differential: A measure can assign any non-negative value; a probability measure is a measure with mu(X) = 1
A measure is defined on a sigma-algebra and is countably additive; an outer measure is defined on all subsets and is only countably subadditive

definition: A sigma-algebra (sigma-field) F on a set X is a collection of subsets of X satisfying: (1) X is in F, (2) if A is in F then its complement X\A is in F, (3) F is closed under countable unions. The pair (X, F) is a measurable space. The Borel sigma-algebra on R^n is generated by open sets. Sigma-algebras provide the domain on which measures are defined.

contrasts.differential: A topology is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections; a sigma-algebra is closed under countable unions and complements. Neither implies the other in general

The power set 2^X is the largest sigma-algebra; the trivial sigma-algebra {empty, X} is the smallest. Measurability restricts attention to a sigma-algebra smaller than the power set to avoid paradoxes (Vitali sets)

definition: A set A is measurable (with respect to a sigma-algebra F) if A is in F. A function f: (X, F) -> (Y, G) is measurable if the preimage of every set in G is in F. Measurability is the analogue of continuity for measure spaces. Measurable functions are those whose 'level sets' can be assigned measure.

contrasts.differential: Continuous functions pull back open sets to open sets; measurable functions pull back measurable sets to measurable sets. Every continuous function is Borel measurable but not conversely
The axiom of choice implies existence of non-measurable sets (Vitali sets). Restricting to a sigma-algebra avoids the paradoxes these sets create

definition: The Lebesgue measure lambda on R^n is the unique complete translation-invariant measure extending the natural notion of volume: lambda([a,b]) = b-a for intervals, lambda(rectangle) = product of side lengths. It is sigma-finite and defined on the Lebesgue sigma-algebra (which properly contains the Borel sigma-algebra). Countable sets have measure zero. The Lebesgue integral generalizes the Riemann integral.

contrasts.differential: Lebesgue measure gives 'length/area/volume'; counting measure counts the number of points in a set
Lebesgue measure on R is infinite (sigma-finite but not finite); a probability measure must total 1. Restricting Lebesgue measure to [0,1] gives a probability measure

definition: A probability measure P on a measurable space (Omega, F) is a measure with P(Omega) = 1. The triple (Omega, F, P) is a probability space. P assigns probabilities to events (sets in F) satisfying: P(Omega) = 1, P(A) >= 0 for all A in F, and countable additivity. Random variables are measurable functions on probability spaces.

contrasts.differential: A general measure can assign any non-negative value including infinity; a probability measure is normalized to total 1
A distribution is the probability measure induced on R (or R^n) by a random variable; a probability measure is the more general concept on any measurable space

definition: A property holds almost everywhere (a.e.) with respect to a measure mu if the set of points where it fails has measure zero. In probability: a property holds almost surely (a.s.) if it holds with probability 1. Two functions equal a.e. are identified in L^p spaces. Almost everywhere equivalence is fundamental to measure-theoretic integration.

contrasts.differential: Everywhere means at every point; almost everywhere allows exceptions on a set of measure zero
A set of measure zero is 'negligible' for integration; almost everywhere means 'except on a set of measure zero'

definition: The Lebesgue integral of a non-negative measurable function f with respect to measure mu is defined as the supremum of integrals of simple functions below f. For general functions, integrate positive and negative parts separately. The Lebesgue integral extends the Riemann integral to a much larger class of functions and enables powerful convergence theorems (dominated convergence, monotone convergence, Fatou's lemma).

contrasts.differential: The Riemann integral partitions the domain; the Lebesgue integral partitions the range. Every Riemann-integrable function is Lebesgue-integrable but not conversely
Summation is integration with respect to counting measure on a discrete set; Lebesgue integration generalizes to arbitrary measure spaces

definition: In measure theory and functional analysis, duality pairs a space with its dual space of linear functionals. Key instances: the Riesz representation theorem identifies the dual of C(X) with the space of signed measures; the dual of L^p is L^q where 1/p + 1/q = 1 (for 1 <= p < infinity). Poincare duality in topology relates H_k and H^{n-k} of an oriented closed n-manifold.

contrasts.differential: L^2 is self-dual (p = q = 2); other L^p spaces are not. A Hilbert space is always self-dual via the Riesz representation
Universal coefficient theorem relates homology and cohomology; Poincare duality relates homology in complementary dimensions on closed manifolds
